findings.headline: Council formally identifies insufficient resources to set balanced budget as significant red risk
findings.detail: In its risk register, the council has flagged as a Net Red (significant) risk that 'the Council has insufficient resources to meet its aspirations and cannot set a balanced budget.' Mitigating actions centre on budget scrutiny and maintaining reserves, suggesting the council is managing structural budget constraints.
findings.matters: A formally identified red risk of budget insufficiency signals the council acknowledges potential structural funding gaps. This is material to credit assessment as it suggests the council may be approaching or at the edge of its financial capacity.
findings.figures: No quantified figures; identified as formal Net Red risk in governance risk register
findings.quote: That the Council has insufficient resources to meet its aspirations and cannot set a balanced budget

findings.headline: Council launching property acquisition programme: £5m long-term fixed-rate borrowing for up to 20 purchases
findings.detail: The council is borrowing £5m over 25-year terms (rates 5.54%-5.86%, maturing 2051) to purchase general fund properties. As of 30 June 2026, £4m had been advanced to acquire 18 properties at total cost of £4,058,318. This represents a strategic expansion of the council's balance sheet into property income dependency.
findings.matters: Long-term fixed-rate property acquisitions require rental income to justify the fixed 25-year debt service. Lenders need clarity on projected yields and how downturns in property values or rental income would affect debt coverage, particularly given the elevated rates locked in.
findings.figures: £5m total; £4m borrowed to date; 18 properties purchased; total cost £4,058,318; rates 5.54%-5.86% maturing 2051
findings.quote: An additional £5,000,000 in total will be borrowed from PWLB to fund the purchase of up to 20 General Fund properties. As of 30 June 2026 £4,000,000 of this has been borrowed

findings.headline: £18m additional borrowing in 2025-26 from deferred capital programme financing, with £26m more required in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council borrowed £18m in 2025-26 explicitly due to deferred capital spending from prior years, and now forecasts a £26m capital financing requirement for 2026-27. This pattern of under-borrowing followed by material acceleration suggests either constrained prior-year finances or a strategic pivot to accelerated capital investment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this borrowing spike reflects sustainable capital investment plans or deferred spending cascading. The pattern of under-borrowing followed by catch-up can signal financial stress or prior austerity.
findings.figures: £18m borrowed in 2025-26; £26m capital financing requirement forecast for 2026-27; three additional PWLB loans of £7m, £6m, and £5m at rates 4.50%-4.62% over three-year terms
findings.quote: The additional borrowing in 2025-2026 was £18,000,000. This is primarily due to the Council not borrowing to fund its capital programme in prior years and existing programme commitments.

findings.paper_title: 1-Cover Report unaudited Statement of Account 2025 26 (Final post SLT) with restatement
findings.headline: Balance sheet for 2023/24 will be restated following auditor challenge of MIRA/LLEP accounting treatment.
findings.detail: The accounting treatment of MIRA/LLEP entries is under active review at auditor request. This will require a restatement of the 2023/24 balance sheet, detailed in Appendix 1, and remains subject to audit approval.
findings.matters: A prior-period restatement signals historical errors in financial reporting and raises questions about the adequacy of financial controls and the reliability of comparative figures.
findings.figures: 2023/24 balance sheet restatement pending
findings.quote: Discussions are currently ongoing relating accounting entries for the MIRA/LLEP. Our existing auditors have requested a review of the previous treatment. Based on this a revised balance sheet for financial year 23/24 will be required.

findings.paper_title: 1-Cover Report unaudited Statement of Account 2025 26 (Final post SLT) with restatement
findings.headline: Auditor will disclaim opinion on 2025/26 accounts due to inherited inability to verify opening balances from prior-year disclaimed opinions.
findings.detail: The previous auditor (EY) issued disclaimed opinions for 2020/21, 2021/22, and 2022/23. The new auditor (Azets) cannot therefore place full assurance on opening balances and will issue a disclaimed audit opinion for 2025/26. The disclaimer may continue through 2026/27, with unmodified opinion only possible from 2027/28.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion provides zero assurance on the financial statements, preventing lenders from relying on the reported financial position, performance, or asset values.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions covering 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2024/25, and 2025/26; potentially extending through 2026/27
findings.quote: Azets issued a disclaimed audit opinion for financial year 2024/25 and will continue to give a disclaimed option in 2025/26. This may also be the case for 2026/27, with the potential for an unmodified opinion in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit - Corporate Governance - Final report (ID 2990169) (1)
findings.headline: Audit Committee governance oversight was significantly weaker historically but has improved sharply in the last 20 months.
findings.detail: The Audit Committee self-assessment score increased from 0.9 out of 5 in September 2024 to 3.9 out of 5 in May 2026. This four-point jump in 20 months reflects substantial historical weaknesses in the committee's capability to provide scrutiny over council governance and risk management, now being addressed through training and improved engagement.
findings.matters: The Audit Committee is the council's primary oversight body for financial and governance controls; a score of 0.9 indicates it was previously unable to provide meaningful scrutiny of financial decisions or management performance—a material risk to lenders.
findings.figures: Self-assessment score: 0.9 out of 5 (September 2024) → 3.9 out of 5 (May 2026)
findings.quote: The Audit Committee produces an annual self-assessment of its governance arrangements. As of the May 2026 update, average scores per question (from zero to five, with five being the best) had increased to 3.9, from a starting point of 0.9 out of 5 in September 2024.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit - Corporate Governance - Final report (ID 2990169) (1)
findings.headline: Employee Code of Conduct training not delivered for five years despite two-year review requirement.
findings.detail: The Employee Code of Conduct has not been updated or retrained since 2021, despite the document itself requiring review every two years. 361 of 410 staff (88%) completed training in 2021, but no refresher training has been delivered since, and new starters receive only a copy of the code, not training. Management response indicates an e-learning module will launch September 1, 2026.
findings.matters: A five-year gap in ethical conduct training creates risk that staff may not understand their obligations around conflicts of interest, gifts, and hospitality—controls particularly material to financial decision-making.
findings.figures: 361 out of 410 staff trained in 2021 (88%); no training delivered 2021–2026
findings.quote: Training has not been delivered to employees since 2021, when the current version of the Code of Conduct was launched.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme shows slippage of £3.075m (30% of budget) carried forward to next year
findings.detail: The council spent £7.376m of a £10.307m General Fund capital budget (71%). HRA capital also shows £0.994m underspent (93% execution rate). Large carry-forwards across both funds indicate projects are not completing to schedule.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage indicates project management challenges, procurement delays, or contractor performance issues; delays service delivery and cash-flow management
findings.figures: £3.075m General Fund carry-forward out of £10.307m budget; £0.994m HRA carry-forward out of £15.716m budget
findings.quote: For the General Fund £7.376m has been spent on capital schemes to the end of March 2026 against a budget of £10.307m... Council will be requested to approve carry forwards totalling £3.075m.

findings.headline: £1.732 million capital for temporary housing acquisitions, crossing into future financial years
findings.detail: The council has allocated £1.732m as a capital carry-forward to purchase properties for temporary housing, described as 'scheme crosses financial years'. This is the largest single capital allocation in the programme and indicates ongoing temporary accommodation demand.
findings.matters: Large capital investment in non-income-generating temporary housing assets indicates significant homelessness demand; creates ongoing maintenance, management and potential void costs
findings.figures: £1,732,660 capital allocation
findings.quote: £1,732,660 - Scheme crosses financial years. Fund set aside to purchase new Properties to assist with temporary housing.

findings.headline: Local Plan submission deadline of 31 December 2026 is four months away with costs still being incurred
findings.detail: The council must submit its Local Plan for independent examination to the Planning Inspectorate by 31 December 2026. Two carry-forwards totalling £146,455 are specifically allocated for consultants preparing evidence studies to meet this deadline. The financial year ends 31 March 2026, leaving only 9 months before the submission date.
findings.matters: Hard statutory deadline; failure results in loss of planning authority status and potential intervention, with serious implications for future revenue and service delivery
findings.figures: Deadline: 31 December 2026; Budget carry-forwards: £146,455 (for evidence studies)
findings.quote: the borough council has to submit the Local Plan for independent examination to the Planning inspectorate by 31 December 2026

findings.headline: £95,310 carried forward for ongoing legal disputes including court appeals and judicial review
findings.detail: The council has reserved £95,310 for legal costs in 2026/27 specifically to cover the Mallory magistrate's court appeal, a linked judicial review, and UN advocacy costs for an Artemis convention challenge. These are unresolved disputes that will continue to generate legal costs.
findings.matters: Multiple unresolved legal disputes indicate governance risk and potential systemic issues; ongoing legal costs reduce financial flexibility
findings.figures: £95,310 carry-forward for legal costs; involves three separate legal actions
findings.quote: Request to carry forward various detail code budgets to help cover legal costs expected in 26/27. This includes the Mallory magistrate's court appeal and the JR linked with Mallory plus UN advocacy costs for the Artemis convention challenge.

findings.headline: Asylum accommodation costs only partially funded by government grant
findings.detail: The council received £108,000 to address increased demand for asylum accommodation support across environmental health, waste and community services. The council explicitly states this funding 'provides a partial contribution towards these cost pressures', meaning the shortfall must be met from general fund resources.
findings.matters: Mandatory cost pressures that cannot be fully funded from government represent unfunded commitments that squeeze either reserves, borrowing capacity, or service delivery
findings.figures: £108,000 government allocation described as covering only part of increased costs
findings.quote: a further baseline allocation of £108,000 related to Asylum accommodation has been confirmed... The funding therefore provides a partial contribution towards these cost pressures

findings.headline: Council Tax collection fell £85,184 short of budget at £5.553m
findings.detail: The council collected £5.553m against a budgeted £5.638m in council tax income, a 1.5% shortfall. Business rates growth exceeded forecast by £107k, but council tax — the larger revenue stream — underperformed, suggesting either collection difficulties or lower property valuations.
findings.matters: Council tax is the revenue base most resistant to external shocks; shortfalls indicate either collection challenges or resident financial stress in the area
findings.figures: £5,553,238 actual vs £5,638,422 budgeted; shortfall £85,184

findings.paper_title: Appendix - MUFG CM - TMSS AIS 200126 - Final Council Version
findings.headline: Treasury advisors explicitly caution interest rate forecasts contain 'hefty caveats' due to multiple economic risks
findings.detail: MUFG notes that while short-term forecasts are robust, medium and long-dated PWLB forecasts carry significant uncertainty from wage growth, geo-political factors, fiscal consolidation risks, Fed policy, and tariff policies. Forecasts for 10-year and 25-50 year PWLB rates have been revised upward 20-50 basis points.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasts are material to borrowing strategy; acknowledged high uncertainty means borrowing costs could exceed the currently projected 4.70% (10-year) and 5.40% (25-year) targets.
findings.figures: Current 10-year PWLB 5.36%, forecast end Q2 2027 4.70%; 25-year current 6.10%, forecast 5.40%
findings.quote: Accordingly, our updated central forecast is made with several hefty caveats. For threats to that central scenario abound.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - MUFG CM - TMSS AIS 200126 - Final Council Version
findings.headline: HRA debt growing 27% to £63.4m by 2028/29, reaching 66% of debt cap
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account debt is forecast to rise from £50.0m to £63.4m by 2028/29 (£13.4m increase), driven by housing capital investment. This brings HRA debt utilisation to 66% of the debt cap (£63.4m against a cap of £95.4m), constraining future housing investment capacity.
findings.matters: HRA debt is secured on rental income; significant growth relative to the cap limits future housing investment and could signal housing revenue pressure.
findings.figures: HRA debt £50.0m (2024/25) rising to £63.4m (2028/29) against cap of £95.4m

findings.paper_title: Appendix - MUFG CM - TMSS AIS 200126 - Final Council Version
findings.headline: Capital receipts collapsing 67% over two years, from £3.1m to £1.0m
findings.detail: Capital receipts (proceeds from asset sales) fall sharply from £3.092m in 2024/25 to £1.007m in 2026/27 and only £600k by 2028/29. This removes a key source of self-funding for capital schemes and increases reliance on borrowing or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Falling capital receipts mean the council has fewer options to fund capital schemes without either borrowing (at currently elevated rates) or burning reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - MUFG CM - TMSS AIS 200126 - Final Council Version
findings.headline: Financing costs rising to 16.87% of net revenue stream by 2026/27, significantly above 2024/25 baseline
findings.detail: Non-HRA financing costs (debt service) rising from 11.64% in 2024/25 to 16.87% in 2026/27 and staying elevated at 17.25% in 2027/28. This trend indicates growing pressure on the revenue budget as debt service consumes an increasing share of resources available for services.
findings.matters: Financing ratios above 15% are commonly considered stress levels; this rising trend reduces financial headroom for revenue pressures or service demand.
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream Non-HRA 11.64 14.80 16.87 17.25

findings.paper_title: Appendix - MUFG CM - TMSS AIS 200126 - Final Council Version
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement to grow £21.7m to £135.6m by 2026/27, with largest annual increase in 2026/27
findings.detail: The CFR (total outstanding capital expenditure not yet paid for) grows from £113.9m to £135.6m by 2026/27. The 2026/27 movement of £15.084m is the sharpest in the forecast, driven by net financing need of £16.846m — the highest in the period.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments ahead signal substantial future borrowing need; the council is managing this by under-borrowing (using reserves) but this depletes the reserve cushion.
findings.figures: CFR rises from £113.943m (2024/25 actual) to £135.611m (2026/27); net financing need £16.846m in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Appendix - MUFG CM - TMSS AIS 200126 - Final Council Version
findings.headline: Fund balances to fall 75% in four years, from £13.1m to £3.16m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's general reserves are declining sharply: £13.061m in 2024/25 actual, falling to £9.673m by 2026/27 and only £3.160m by 2028/29. This reflects the council's strategy of using reserves to fund capital schemes rather than borrowing, but leaves minimal buffer for revenue pressures or unexpected costs.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves significantly constrain a council's financial flexibility; at £3.16m the council would have little cushion for in-year overspends or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: £13.061m (2024/25 actual) declining to £3.160m (2028/29 estimate) — a 76% reduction
findings.quote: Fund balances / reserves 13,061 12,194 9,673 6,772 3,160

findings.headline: Significant compliance and capital surveys required on aging housing stock
findings.detail: Housing Repairs budget includes £357,400 of new spending for regulatory compliance and condition assessment: asbestos surveys (£30,000), stock condition surveys (£50,000), accelerated EPC programme (£30,000), updated electrical safety work (£12,000), and additional site maintenance for disposal preparation (£100,000). These indicate substantial aging stock requiring major compliance investment.
findings.matters: Signals aging housing stock with escalating compliance and maintenance demands; may require continued elevated capital spending and borrowing beyond current plans.
findings.figures: Total repairs growth £357,400; asbestos surveys £30,000; stock condition survey £50,000; EPC programme £30,000; electrical safety £12,000; site maintenance £100,000
findings.quote: Due to changes in legislation and additional demands, growths of £357,400 have been included within the repairs budget. Additional staffing and vehicle resource for In-house contractor (2 year fixed term contracts) 97,000; Stock condition survey work 50,000; Accelerated EPC programme 30,000; Updated electrical safety regulation 12,000; Asbestos surveys 30,000

findings.headline: Service charge income underperforming against budget in current year
findings.detail: The 2025/26 revised budget shows shortfalls in ancillary service charges: garage rents down £16,000 and sheltered scheme charges down £33,000. This suggests actual tenant income is coming in below forecast, either from reduced uptake or collection difficulties.
findings.matters: Indicates the council's service income forecasting may be optimistic, or tenants may be stretching affordability; affects cash flow and may signal affordability pressures in the tenant base.
findings.figures: Garage rent shortfall £16,000; sheltered scheme service charge shortfall £33,000
findings.quote: Shortfall garage rents 16,000 [and] Shortfall in sheltered scheme service charges 33,000

findings.headline: Maximum rent increase is critical to meeting service priorities
findings.detail: The council is applying the 4.8% maximum permitted rent increase (CPI plus 1%) and explicitly states this level is essential to fund operations. The rent increase generates an additional £823,980 in income that the council says is 'required in order that service priorities can be met including: Meeting decent homes standard, Meeting compliance and regulation requirements, Continuing with decarbonisation works.'
findings.matters: Shows the council has limited budget flexibility and is operating at the permitted ceiling for tenant income; if rents cannot increase further or tenants cannot afford them, the council would struggle to fund maintenance and services.
findings.figures: 4.8% rent increase; rental income forecast £16,507,290 (up £823,980)
findings.quote: It is critical we use this rate to maximise income through applying this rent increase. This is required in order that service priorities can be met including: Meeting decent homes standard, Meeting compliance and regulation requirements

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 and Capital Strategy V2 - formatted - Council Version
findings.headline: Council states it will find carbon emergency targets increasingly unaffordable due to financial pressure
findings.detail: In the climate implications section, the council explicitly states that 'The financial pressure on the council will mean it become increasing difficult to meet its carbon emergency targets by 2030.' This is a statement from the finance function acknowledging that corporate strategic targets are unaffordable.
findings.matters: An explicit acknowledgement that strategic corporate targets are unaffordable signals material budget pressure and difficult prioritization ahead. A finance director and lender would view this as a warning that further savings or service cuts may be necessary to balance budgets.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The financial pressure on the council will mean it become increasing difficult to meet its carbon emergency targets by 2030.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 and Capital Strategy V2 - formatted - Council Version
findings.headline: Bradgate Stables listed building: council may be forced into unplanned spending if owner fails to maintain urgent works
findings.detail: Bradgate Stables is a Grade II* Listed Building on the Historic England at Risk Register. The council has enforced voluntary undertaking of urgent works by the owner but retains the option to carry out works 'in default' if the owner does not continue. The council has budgeted £300k (with 80% Historic England grant) but states 'if the progress is not satisfactory then the Council may need to progress with in default works during 2026'.
findings.matters: This creates a potential unplanned call on council funds if the private building owner fails to maintain works. Enforcement costs are difficult to predict and could exceed the budgeted amount, particularly if the works are more extensive than anticipated.
findings.figures: Budgeted cost £300k; Historic England grant £240k; Council element £60k
findings.quote: The council have enforced the voluntary undertaking of Urgent Works by the building owner, but should these not be continued the council have the option of commissioning required works in default and then seeking to claim back costs from the owner... if the progress is not satisfactory then the Council may need to progress with in default works during 2026

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 and Capital Strategy V2 - formatted - Council Version
findings.headline: Jubilee Depot cost overruns: £1m of additional costs identified during programme refresh
findings.detail: The Jubilee Depot scheme has been rephased with increased costs of £300k in 2025/26 and £747k in 2026/27 (total £1.047m). The scheme is described as having 'Increased costs of works', indicating scope changes or construction inflation during planning.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on individual schemes during programme development suggest either project estimation issues or construction inflation. A lender would want to understand whether other schemes in the capital programme carry similar unidentified cost risks.
findings.figures: Jubilee Depot increased costs: £300k in 2025/26, £747k in 2026/27
findings.quote: Jubilee Depot  300 747 0 Increased costs of works

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 and Capital Strategy V2 - formatted - Council Version
findings.headline: Capital Receipts Reserve depleted by £4.4m over four years as council uses proceeds to repay debt
findings.detail: The Capital Receipts Reserve is forecast to fall from £9.0m to £4.6m by 2028/29. In 2025/26 alone, £3.2m will be used to repay prior debt. The document warns that failure to pay off this debt will result in additional MRP costs charged to the general fund from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion and debt repayment from capital receipts signals reduced financial headroom and indicates the council is using capital proceeds for debt management rather than investment. The warning of additional MRP costs indicates future revenue pressure.
findings.figures: Opening Capital Receipts Reserve 2025/26: £8,998k; Closing balance 2028/29: £4,606k; Debt repayment from receipts 2025/26: £3,235k
findings.quote: It is estimated that £3.235m will be used in 2025/26 to reduce the Council's overall borrowing position. Failure to pay off this debt will result in an additional MRP cost chargeable to the general fund from 2026/27 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 and Capital Strategy V2 - formatted - Council Version
findings.headline: Finance team explicitly acknowledges that financing options are becoming restricted over the medium term
findings.detail: The Capital Strategy contains a specific statement that 'availability of financing options is becoming restricted over the medium term as asset sales become less frequent and the availability of funding from central government becomes restricted.' This appears twice in the strategy (sections 3.17 and 3.36), emphasizing the constraint.
findings.matters: A finance director's explicit acknowledgement of constrained funding capacity is a key planning signal indicating realistic forecasting and that future capital programmes will be under pressure. This is not generic commentary but a specific assessment from the council's finance function.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The availability of financing options is becoming restricted over the medium term as asset sales become less frequent and the availability of funding from central government becomes restricted.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 and Capital Strategy V2 - formatted - Council Version
findings.headline: Right to Buy receipts declining sharply, from £3.1m to £375k annually by 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's Right to Buy capital receipts are forecast to collapse from £3.1m in 2025/26 to £375k in both 2027/28 and 2028/29. These receipts have historically funded HRA capital investment, and their decline significantly constrains the HRA's future financing options.
findings.matters: Declining RTB receipts reduce the council's financial flexibility for housing investment. A lender would want to model whether remaining funding sources can support the proposed HRA capital programme of £58m over four years.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 and Capital Strategy V2 - formatted - Council Version
findings.headline: Two major capital schemes cancelled during programme refresh: Solar Panels and New Crematorium
findings.detail: The council has removed the £1m Council Offices Solar Panel Scheme and the £4m New Crematorium from the capital programme. Both are listed in the rephasing schedule as 'Proposed scheme no longer proceeding'. These represent £5m of previously-planned investment that has been cut.
findings.matters: Capital scheme cancellations signal budget recalibration or constraint and show the council stepping back from regeneration and service delivery ambitions that were previously committed enough to appear in a prior-year programme.
findings.figures: Council Offices Solar Panel Scheme: £1m cancelled; New Crematorium: £4m cancelled
findings.quote: Council Offices Solar Panel Scheme -1,000 0 0 Proposed scheme no longer proceeding... New Crematorium -4,000 0 0 Proposed scheme no longer proceeding

findings.headline: Government notified the council of material financial settlement changes only days before the budget meeting
findings.detail: The Government communicated significant changes to the financial settlement in late December, just days before the scheduled budget meeting. The council explicitly states these changes are material and to the council's detriment.
findings.matters: Late-notice funding changes create execution risk and reduce the council's ability to plan with certainty; the adversarial framing ('to the detriment') suggests the council views the change as damaging
findings.figures: Changes notified 2025/26 to 2027/28 period
findings.quote: Government only notified us of significant changes to the financial settlement just days before the scheduled budget meeting. Those changes are material to the forecast position provided only in late December and are to the detriment of HBBC

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation by April 2028 will require a 10-year recovery plan to restore financial balance
findings.detail: The council is planning a district-led local government reorganisation by 1 April 2028, which it acknowledges will require a 10-year plan for the new Unitary authority to bring finances into balance.
findings.matters: The council cannot fix its deficit within normal planning horizons and requires structural reorganisation; this is a material change to the organisation and a long-term planning horizon
findings.figures: 1 April 2028; 10-year plan
findings.quote: local government reorganisation (LGR) in this MTFS by 1 April 2028, and... there is a 10 year plan for the new Unitary to bring finances into balance

findings.headline: Reserves will be heavily used to manage a structural deficit across the MTFS period
findings.detail: The council's MTFS incorporates a deficit position and expects to draw down reserves significantly. The council has already modelled this deficit into the financial submission for district-led local government reorganisation.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is not sustainable and signals the council cannot balance spending and income through normal measures; this is a structural problem, not a cyclical one
findings.figures: Deficit position incorporated in LGR submission; no specific reserve amount given
findings.quote: reserves will be heavily used. A deficit position (as at the end of this MTFS period) has already been incorporated into the financial modelling for the District led LGR submission

findings.headline: The council is losing all of its £4.6m retained business rates growth due to the 2026/27 business rates reset
findings.detail: The business rates reset eliminates the council's accumulated retained business rates growth, a material loss of recurring revenue. This compounds other pressures from declining government support and rising costs.
findings.matters: This is a permanent loss of a major recurring income stream that the council had been relying on, reducing financial flexibility
findings.figures: £4.6m retained business rates growth
findings.quote: a business rates reset for 2026/27, which means the Council is losing all of its £4.6 retained business rates growth

findings.headline: Enterprise zone forward funding arrangement at risk from government's business rates reset
findings.detail: The council has a forward funding agreement for enterprise zone business rates based on the previous business rates retention method. Government's reset may change how enterprise zone growth is shared, potentially triggering unexpected losses on the council's arrangement, though the final impact is still being analyzed.
findings.matters: Enterprise zone revenue has been treated as a growth opportunity. Changes to the allocation mechanism could unexpectedly reduce income and be difficult to offset, adding to the structural deficit.
findings.figures: Forward funding amount not disclosed; government reset methodology still being finalized
findings.quote: The change could lead to losses on the arrangement.

findings.headline: Net budget gap of £2.8m in 2026/27 with no identified savings to close it
findings.detail: After all government transitional support and planned savings, the council faces an unfunded gap of £2.8m in 2026/27. The MTFS shows zero savings or new income needed only because this gap is being plugged by drawing down reserves, not by sustainable cost control.
findings.matters: A growing budget gap not covered by savings indicates the council is consuming reserves faster than sustainable. Future years will require explicit service cuts or significant new income, neither of which has been identified.
findings.figures: Total pressures: £5.9m; reductions and savings actioned: £2.3m; unfunded gap: £2.8m for 2026/27
findings.quote: Overall, growths and pressures exceed savings and new income by £2.8m for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Payroll costs rising sharply (£2.1m in one year) with further pressures unconfirmed
findings.detail: National pay settlements and new posts required for food waste have driven payroll costs up by £2.1m in a single year. The council notes that final national pay agreements are not yet confirmed, creating further unquantified risk to the budget.
findings.matters: Payroll is typically the largest service cost and the hardest to cut once committed. Uncontrolled pay growth directly reduces service capacity and leaves little room for absorbing other pressures.
findings.figures: Payroll 2025/26: £15.6m; payroll 2026/27: £17.7m; increase: £2.1m; additional unconfirmed pay pressures: ~£1.3m
findings.quote: National pay settlements and new posts for food waste have increased payroll costs sharply (from £15.6m in 2025/26 £17.7m in 2026/27).

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs and demand far exceed available government funding
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation costs are rising sharply, with the budget increased to £2.1m in 2025/26 and forecast at £1.5m in 2026/27, but government funding available is only £0.54m. This leaves an unfunded gap of approximately £1.0m that must be met from reserves or other savings.
findings.matters: Homelessness and temporary housing demand is rising and is not being funded by government, forcing councils to meet the open-ended pressure from their own resources, exhausting reserves faster.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation costs 2026/27: £1.5m; government funding: £0.54m; unfunded gap: ~£0.96m
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation costs have increased, the budget was increased to £2.1m in 2025/26 and is almost £1.5m in 2026/27, but government funding is only £0.54m.

findings.headline: Food waste implementation costs of £1.45m far outstrip government funding
findings.detail: New national food waste collection requirements are mandated but government funding covers only a portion of implementation cost. The council must absorb an unfunded gap of approximately £0.88m from existing budgets.
findings.matters: This is a statutory requirement imposed with insufficient funding, creating new unfunded pressure and reducing budget flexibility for other council services.
findings.figures: Food waste implementation cost: £1.45m; additional government funding for this: £1.45m (but distributed across all food waste, temporary accommodation, and pay pressures)
findings.quote: the implementation of food waste costs alone are £1.45m

findings.headline: Council likely to hand a deficit position to the new unitary authority in 2028
findings.detail: The financial position is unsustainable beyond 2028. The council explicitly identifies in its own risk register that it is highly likely to transfer a deficit to the successor unitary authority when local government reorganisation completes, forcing the new authority to inherit inherited debt and structural pressures.
findings.matters: A deficit handover indicates failure of financial management within the council's lifetime and means the new unitary authority will start operations compromised, unable to invest in services or respond to demands.
findings.figures: All earmarked reserves exhausted by 31 March 2028; LGR implementation 1 April 2028
findings.quote: The Council is highly likely to transfer a deficit position to any new unitary authority in place from 1 April 2028.

findings.headline: Structural deficit requires spending of all earmarked reserves by March 2028
findings.detail: The council has a structural deficit where income and government funding do not cover expenditure. The MTFS relies on depleting all earmarked reserves to balance the budget, reducing them from £5.5m (2025/26) to just £250k (2028). If local government reorganisation is delayed, no balanced budget is achievable in 2028/29.
findings.matters: Reserves provide financial resilience for unexpected costs and shocks. Their near-total depletion before the change to unitary authority leaves zero contingency for the transition and creates systemic financial fragility.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves declining from £5.5m (2025/26) to £3.2m (2026/27) to £250k (2028); structural deficit £1.8m to £2.8m annually
findings.quote: all earmarked reserves will be used by the 31 March 2028

findings.headline: Business Rates Reset in 2026/27 will eliminate £4.6m of retained growth
findings.detail: The council faces loss of all retained business rates growth in 2026/27, described as a major financial stability risk. Additionally, the enterprise zone funding arrangement may be affected by government's new method of business rates allocation, potentially triggering further losses.
findings.matters: Loss of £4.6m is nearly a third of the council's annual net service expenditure and creates a structural funding gap that cannot be easily replaced.
findings.figures: £4.6m retained business rates growth to be lost; 3.4% year-on-year reduction in core funding
findings.quote: The Council will lose all of its £4.6m retained business rates growth, a major risk to financial stability.

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Car parking income underperforming; potential £0.2–0.3m lost revenue opportunity
findings.detail: Fees have not kept pace with RPI inflation since 2011/12. Analysis shows parking could generate £0.2–0.3m more annually if prices had tracked inflation. No plans to raise fees are included in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Underutilised revenue source that could ease reserve pressure; absence of fee increases suggests political constraint on raising charges.
findings.figures: Potential lost income: £0.2–0.3m annually; example: short-stay 1-hour fee £0.60 vs RPI-indexed £1.10 (83% shortfall)
findings.quote: To improve income performance consideration would need to be given to increasing the car parking fees

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Section 114 (insolvency) risk explicitly cited if savings targets are not met
findings.detail: Document warns that failure to achieve savings 'might lead to the risk of a S114 recommendation potentially being needed at some point in the future'. This is an explicit acknowledgment of insolvency risk. Support via capital flexibilities is positioned as conditional on a financial improvement plan.
findings.matters: Section 114 notice is a formal insolvency declaration; lenders and auditors would need to consider this council a higher credit risk.
findings.figures: No specific amounts, but the risk is linked to unforeseen cost pressures or failure to deliver £2–3m+ annual savings
findings.quote: failure to achieve savings, due to any unseen circumstance, might lead to the risk of a S114 recommendation potentially being needed at some point in the future

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Government transitional relief (damping) support only guaranteed to end of 2028/29
findings.detail: £2.1m damping in 2027/28 is helping offset RSG reductions. However, damping is only committed to 2028/29, and a new unitary would need to absorb any further RSG cuts after that point. The document explicitly notes combined RSG + damping falls by £327k in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Temporary support masks an underlying structural problem; when support ends, the unitary may face a more severe deficit than currently visible.
findings.figures: Damping 2026/27: £534k; 2027/28: £2.115m; year-on-year change 2027/28: −£327k; RSG decline 2027/28: £1.9m offset by damping increase
findings.quote: Damping, although increasing to offset most, but not all, of the reduction in RSG, is only included until the end of 2028/29

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: LGR merger costs unknown but reserved amount (£0.25m) may be insufficient
findings.detail: Council has set aside £0.25m for local government reorganisation costs in April 2028. This is not based on specific planning, only that 'other areas have incurred substantial cost'. Actual costs could be significantly higher.
findings.matters: Unforeseen LGR costs could force additional reserve draws or borrowing, or require the new unitary to absorb the shortfall.
findings.figures: LGR reserve: £250k; costs assumed substantial but not quantified
findings.quote: A reserve of £0.25m has been set aside in the MTFS to help deal with any costs that maybe incurred due to the reorganisation. This is not based on any specific information other than it is prudent to make some provision as other areas have incurred substantial cost

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Pay costs not yet agreed; 1% variance adds £0.5m unfunded cost
findings.detail: MTFS assumes 3.2% pay award in 2026/27 but settlement is not yet agreed. A 1% variance from assumption would cost an additional £0.5m over the MTFS period. Actual inflation may exceed assumption.
findings.matters: Pay costs are the largest single budget item; unfunded pay awards consume reserves or force service cuts mid-year.
findings.figures: Assumed pay award: 3.2% (2026/27), 3% thereafter; 1% variance = £0.5m additional cost over MTFS period; current pay budget: £17.8m (2026/27)
findings.quote: the pay settlement for 2026/27 is not yet known, therefore this could be more if a higher pay award is negotiated nationally. If the settlement is 1% higher for 2026/27, the this would add about £0.5m to the pay costs

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Leicestershire business rates pool closing in 2026/27, ending £2.75m annual subsidy
findings.detail: The pool released £2.8m to HBBC cumulatively and £1m in 2025/26 alone. After the business rates reset, the pool is no longer financially viable and closes. This £2.75m loss is already included in the MTFS deficit position.
findings.matters: Loss of this subsidy was predictable but the reset timing removes a key funding source; any delay to reset beyond 2028/29 would create unforeseen cash pressures.
findings.figures: Pool levy: £2.75m in 2025/26; cumulative benefit 2021/22–2025/26: £4m; returned to HBBC in 2025/26: £1m
findings.quote: The changes to the business rate position across the local area, will mean that the local business rate pool arrangement will not be financially viable and will be closed in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation budget pressure of £0.95m unfunded by government
findings.detail: In-year supplementary of £0.9m needed in 2025/26. 2026/27 budget is £1.5m but government funding only £0.54m, leaving a £0.95m gap. Original 2025/26 baseline was £1m. This is a growing demand pressure being carried by the council.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory duty but unfunded; the gap must be covered from general fund or reserves, adding to the structural deficit.
findings.figures: 2025/26 budget: £2.1m (includes £0.9m in-year increase); 2026/27: £1.5m budget vs £0.54m government funding; funding gap circa £0.95m
findings.quote: The budget was increased to £2.1m in 2025/26 and is almost £1.5m in 2026/27, but government funding is only £0.54m

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Loss of £4.6m annual business rates growth in 2026/27 from government reset
findings.detail: Business rates reset removes all retained growth and increases the tariff HBBC pays to government from £12.1m to £19.2m. This is described as a 'major risk to financial stability'. The council will be in a 'safety net position' throughout the MTFS period, meaning insufficient rates to cover baseline allocation.
findings.matters: Loss of recurring income of this scale requires either spending cuts, reserves depletion, or new income; the safety net position removes flexibility on business rates.
findings.figures: Business rates growth loss: £4.6m; tariff increase: £7.2m (from £12.1m to £19.2m); council in safety net position with negative rates retained (−£53k in 2026/27)
findings.quote: The council will lose all its £4.6m retained business rates growth, a major risk to financial stability

findings.paper_title: MTFS full document for Council v9a
findings.headline: Structural deficit with almost complete reserve depletion by 2028
findings.detail: The council's income from all sources does not cover expenditure. Earmarked reserves of £5.5m are forecast to fall to £250k by March 2028. The council is balancing budgets by drawing down reserves, which is unsustainable if the reset is delayed beyond 2028.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion indicates the council cannot sustain services without reducing costs or raising income; a delayed merger would force difficult decisions or potential insolvency declarations.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £5.5m (2026) → £3.2m (2027) → £250k (2028); deficit in 2027/28 alone is £4.9m before reserve use
findings.quote: almost all the Council's earmarked reserves will be used by 2027/28. If LGR is delayed this position could not be continued into 2028/29 as all earmarked reserves would have been used

findings.headline: Current PWLB borrowing rates are elevated at 4.78-6.10%, with advisor warnings that rates may remain high despite forecasts for falls.
findings.detail: The council's treasury advisors forecast PWLB rates will fall from current levels by Q2 2027. However, they explicitly warn of significant downside risks, stating that 'medium to longer gilt yields will not remain at elevated levels' only if inflation moderates as expected. Multiple risks are identified: weak economic growth, potential fiscal tightening requiring government borrowing, geopolitical factors, and changed pension fund behaviour.
findings.matters: If rates remain elevated rather than falling as forecast, the cost of financing the £114m debt portfolio will be materially higher than budgeted, with impacts cascading through the revenue budget.
findings.figures: PWLB Certainty Rates (11 August 2025): 5-year 4.78%, 10-year 5.36%, 25-year 6.10%, 50-year 5.87%
findings.quote: we see no obvious reason why medium to longer gilt yields will not remain at elevated levels, even allowing for a gradual reduction in inflation over the course of the forecast

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 26% over four years, requiring external debt to rise from £79m to £114m.
findings.detail: The council's capital borrowing need (CFR) is forecast to grow from £113.943m to £143.888m between 2024/25 and 2028/29. To fund this, external debt will increase from £79.34m to £114.262m. The council is deliberately reducing its 'under-borrowed' position, meaning it will increasingly rely on market borrowing rather than reserves.
findings.matters: A 43% increase in external debt over four years, combined with minimal reserves, creates refinancing and interest rate exposure that could materially impact the council's revenue budget.
findings.figures: Total CFR £113,943m (2024/25) to £143,888m (2028/29); External debt £79,340m to £114,262m; Additional borrowing required £11-22m per year
findings.quote: The Authority is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves planned to decline to minimal levels by 2028/29, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.detail: The council's general fund balance is forecast to decline from £13.061m in 2024/25 to £3.160m by 2028/29. This 76% reduction reflects the council using reserves to fund capital expenditure and offset borrowing needs. By 2028/29, the council will have very limited reserve buffers.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves restrict the council's ability to respond to unexpected costs or revenue shocks, and severely limit operational and strategic flexibility.
findings.figures: Fund balances decline from £13,061k (2024/25 actual) to £3,160k (2028/29 estimate)
findings.quote: Year End Resources: Fund balances / reserves 13,061 (2024/25 Actual)... 3,160 (2028/29 Estimate)

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation will end this council's existence and merge it into a unitary by April 2028
findings.detail: The government has mandated reorganisation of all two-tier council areas. This council will cease to exist as a separate entity on 1 April 2028, merging with six other Leicestershire councils into South Leicestershire Unitary Council. Three alternative proposals are still being considered.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that this council will cease to be the borrower and service provider in less than 3 years. The debt arrangements will transfer to the new unitary council, with uncertainty until the government confirms which proposal will proceed.
findings.figures: Reorganisation effective 1 April 2028
findings.quote: This would mean on the 1 April 2028 Hinckley and Bosworth would become part of a new South Leicestershire Unitary Council if our proposal was successful. Other proposals are being returned to Government by Leicestershire County Council and Leicester City Council.

findings.headline: Pension liability of £8.3m constrains financial flexibility despite year-on-year improvement
findings.detail: The council has a net pension liability of £8.3m (improved from £9.6m prior year) representing the long-term cost of staff pensions. The council must continue making contributions to the pension fund. Any underperformance of pension assets would worsen the position.
findings.matters: This is a material balance sheet liability that limits the council's financial flexibility. Approximately 6% of the council's annual budget requirement is committed to addressing this liability over time.
findings.figures: £8.3m net pension liability (down from £9.6m prior year)
findings.quote: Note 36 discloses a net pension liability of £8,327 million for the Council as at 31st March 2025 compared to £9.584 million at the March 2024.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs surged by £500,000 in one year
findings.detail: The council incurred net additional bed and breakfast costs of £500,000 in 2024/25 to address homelessness. The council also lists 'Increased homelessness presentations and temporary accommodation requirements' as a corporate risk, suggesting this cost pressure is expected to persist.
findings.matters: This is a rapidly growing cost that the council cannot easily reduce without solving underlying homelessness. It represents structural demand pressure that will continue consuming resources.
findings.figures: £500,000 additional B&B costs in 2024/25
findings.quote: Net Additional Bed and Breakfast Costs - £500,000

findings.headline: Business rates reset in 2026/27 will create a £3.45m fiscal cliff in 2027/28
findings.detail: The government plans to reset the business rates retention system in 2026/27. The council has calculated this will require £3.45m of new income or savings in 2027/28, subject to ongoing consultation. The council has only received a one-year settlement for 2025/26, adding uncertainty.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand this material gap in the medium-term finances. If the council cannot identify £3.45m of savings or new income, it will need to either cut services or increase borrowing.
findings.figures: £3.45m new income or savings required in 2027/28
findings.quote: with a potential need for new income and savings of £3.45m in 2027/28. However, there in ongoing consultation with government nationally, and changes may yet be made that would reduce or remove this requirement.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Draft Internal Audit Annual Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: Follow-up audit of previous recommendations deferred - implementation verification gap
findings.detail: The council did not complete follow-up audits during 2024/25 to verify whether recommendations from prior audits were actually implemented. This work has been carried forward to the 2025-26 audit plan, creating a gap in understanding whether identified control weaknesses were remedied.
findings.matters: Without verified follow-up on implementation, a lender cannot be confident that the council is materially addressing control weaknesses, only that management accepted the recommendations
findings.figures: 5 planned follow-up days deferred from 2024/25 to 2025/26
findings.quote: Follow up of recommendations raised was not carried out during 2024/25 and has been carried forward to 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Draft Internal Audit Annual Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: Council's overall audit opinion is Moderate - governance improvements required
findings.detail: The overall audit opinion is Moderate, indicating that some improvements are required to enhance the adequacy and effectiveness of governance, risk management and control. Of 9 reviews, 1 received Substantial assurance, 6 Moderate, and 2 Limited. Total of 35 recommendations were raised (increase from 28 in prior year).
findings.matters: A Moderate audit opinion combined with control weaknesses in capital and IT governance indicates the council has material control environment issues that could impair financial management
findings.figures: 1 Substantial, 6 Moderate, 2 Limited assurance opinions; 35 total recommendations (1 high, 21 medium, 13 low priority)
findings.quote: our opinion on the framework of governance, risk management, and control is Moderate in its overall adequacy and effectiveness.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Draft Internal Audit Annual Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: Capital Programme audit identified control weaknesses requiring corrective action
findings.detail: The Capital Programme audit received Limited assurance opinion, meaning control weaknesses have been noted that require corrective action for the control framework to operate effectively. Six recommendations were raised and all accepted by management. The audit required 3 additional days beyond the planned 12 days due to delays in starting.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in capital programme governance are material to a lender assessing the council's ability to manage major projects and capital spend
findings.figures: 6 recommendations raised; audit took 15 actual days vs 12 planned
findings.quote: Control weaknesses have been noted that require corrective action if the control framework is to be considered as operating effectively.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Draft Internal Audit Annual Report - 2024-25
findings.headline: IT Vulnerability Management audit contains the one high priority control weakness exposing council to unacceptable residual risk
findings.detail: The IT Vulnerability Management audit received Limited assurance and contains the single high priority recommendation raised across all audits, along with 3 medium and 2 low priority recommendations. As of this report in January 2026, the review remains in draft awaiting management comments.
findings.matters: An unresolved high priority IT governance or security weakness of unacceptable risk level could impair the council's financial management systems and business continuity
findings.figures: 1 high priority recommendation, 3 medium priority, 2 low priority
findings.quote: The IT review remains in draft as we are awaiting management comments.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease standard implementation not completed; auditors unable to test lease asset and liability disclosures
findings.detail: IFRS 16 was a new standard for 2024/25 requiring councils to record right-of-use assets and lease liabilities on the balance sheet. Auditors identified this as a high-risk accounting estimate but could not complete testing because 'management did not provide appropriate and sufficient audit evidence in time.' This new significant accounting area remains unaudited.
findings.matters: Unaudited accounting for leases means a category of assets and liabilities on the balance sheet has no independent verification. Material lease commitments could be misclassified or misstated.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 identified as high inherent risk of material misstatement (valuation; completeness). Work incomplete at audit sign-off.
findings.quote: We have started but not been able to conclude our work as management did not provide appropriate and sufficient audit evidence in time to allow us to test the disclosures within the accounts.

findings.headline: Working paper quality rated AMBER; auditors experienced systemic delays in obtaining audit evidence
findings.detail: The auditors rated the quality of working papers and management's adherence to audit timetable as AMBER (developing), noting 'delays in obtaining working papers and sufficient audit evidence for a number of audit areas' that impacted their ability to complete testing and build back assurance over prior years.
findings.matters: Repeated delays in responding to auditors indicate a finance function under pressure or lacking adequate capacity and systems. This is predictive of financial control weakness and risk of undetected errors.
findings.figures: Quality indicator grading: AMBER for working papers and timetable adherence.
findings.quote: We experienced delays in obtaining working papers and sufficient audit evidence for a number of audit areas. This impacted our ability to complete work on these balances for 2024/25 and has resulted in further delays in our ability to build back assurance.

findings.headline: No assurance over pension liability valuation (£8.3m) due to missing prior year audit evidence
findings.detail: Auditors performed no work on the council's pension assets and liabilities valuation due to absence of assurance over opening balances from prior disclaimed years. The pension liability is a significant estimate (£8,327k) but has no audit trail back to the last triennial valuation. Auditors note they cannot verify membership data, year-on-year movements, or the current year valuation.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are often a council's largest contingent liability. Without audit verification, the reported position is unverified and could mask significant swings in unfunded liabilities affecting long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Pension assets and liabilities: £8,327k in the 2024/25 accounts. No assurance available due to 4-year audit gap.
findings.quote: we have not been provided with assurance by the pension fund auditor over membership of the pension fund back to the last triennial valuation. This means we have no assurance on the movements in year and cannot gain sufficient audit evidence on the material accuracy of the valuation of the pension fund liability as at 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Council's audit opinion will be disclaimed for the fifth consecutive year
findings.detail: The auditors plan to disclaim their opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, unable to form an opinion on whether the accounts give a true and fair view. This follows disclaimed opinions for 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24. The auditors state they cannot verify opening balances or complete sufficient testing on key accounting estimates due to time constraints and lack of prior year assurance.
findings.matters: A disclaimer means the council's financial position, including reported reserves and asset values, has not been independently verified. For lenders, this means no verified picture of the council's financial health; for the finance director, this represents failure to meet statutory financial reporting requirements.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2020/21–2024/25). Materiality threshold £1,091k.
findings.quote: it has not been possible to regain full assurance, and it is not possible for us to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026. The limitations imposed from this lack of assurance on opening balances and closing balances in key areas means we are unable to form an opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. We therefore intend to disclaim our opinion.

news_drafts.headline: Council formally identifies insufficient resources to set balanced budget as significant red risk
news_drafts.lead: A formally identified red risk of budget insufficiency signals the council acknowledges potential structural funding gaps. This is material to credit assessment as it suggests the council may be approaching or at the edge of its financial capacity.

news_drafts.headline: Council launching property acquisition programme: £5m long-term fixed-rate borrowing for up to 20 purchases
news_drafts.lead: Long-term fixed-rate property acquisitions require rental income to justify the fixed 25-year debt service. Lenders need clarity on projected yields and how downturns in property values or rental income would affect debt coverage, particularly given the…

news_drafts.headline: £18m additional borrowing in 2025-26 from deferred capital programme financing, with £26m more required in 2026-27
news_drafts.lead: A lender needs to understand whether this borrowing spike reflects sustainable capital investment plans or deferred spending cascading. The pattern of under-borrowing followed by catch-up can signal financial stress or prior austerity.
